pos: n. (the primatial see of all Ireland, held after the Reformation by two rival lines of archbishops)
etymology: From Irish Ard Mhacha, the height of Macha; ard, a height, and the personal name Macha.
biblical_def: Armagh is the oldest see in Ireland, traditionally Patrick's own foundation, and its archbishop has been Primate of All Ireland since the twelfth century. At the Reformation the crown's appointments carried the see into the Church of Ireland, while Rome continued to appoint archbishops of Armagh of its own, so that from the sixteenth century there have been two lines claiming the same chair and the same primacy — an arrangement that still obtains. George Dowdall left rather than conform under Edward VI and returned under Mary; Hugh Goodacre was consecrated and dead within months; and later James Ussher made the see a centre of serious learning. The dictionary records Armagh because the contest over it was a contest about primacy itself, and the Lord's words on titles and rank are the measure of every such claim: “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a primate as the chief ecclesiastic in a national church; preeminence as superiority, precedence; and an ensample as an example, a pattern or model for imitation.
webster_full: PRIMATE, n. [L. primas.] The chief ecclesiastic in the church; an archbishop who presides over other bishops.
PREEMINENCE, n. Superiority in excellence; distinction above others in rank; precedence.
ENSAMPLE, n. An example; a pattern or model for imitation.
HERITAGE, n. [L. haereditas.] Inheritance; an estate that passes by descent; in Scripture, the people of God.
BRETHREN, n. plural of brother; members of the same society, or of the same Christian body.
scriptures: Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
I wrote unto the church: but Diotrephes, who loveth to have the preeminence among them, receiveth us not.
corruption_summary: The primatial see of all Ireland, traditionally Patrick's foundation, claimed since the Reformation by rival Church of Ireland and Roman lines of archbishops.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live question is an old one and it is not settled by preferring whichever line one belongs to. Two men have held the title Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland at the same time for four and a half centuries, each regarding the other as no archbishop. The dictionary's own confession denies that any such office is of divine institution at all, and therefore denies the premise of the whole dispute; it also declines to pretend the dispute was over nothing, since what was at stake was who had authority over the churches of a nation.

The principle to recover is the Lord's plain prohibition of ecclesiastical rank as a category, given with a reason attached: “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). Greatness in his kingdom is inverted by definition — “But he that is greatest among you shall be your servant” (Mat 23:11). Peter, of all men, forbids elders to lord it over the flock: “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). And John names the appetite itself in one word: Diotrephes “loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9).

“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — the contest was over authority in a nation's churches.
“who loveth to have the preeminence among them” (3Jn 1:9) — the Primacy of All Ireland, held since the twelfth century.

pos: n. (the Munster archbishopric on the Rock of Cashel, held for fifty years by a man who also held Roman sees)
etymology: From Irish Caiseal, a stone fort or ring-wall, itself from Latin castellum, a castle.
biblical_def: Cashel is the limestone outcrop in Tipperary that was the seat of the kings of Munster and then of an archbishopric, with its cathedral, round tower and chapel still standing on the rock. At the Reformation the see passed to the Church of Ireland, and from 1571 to 1622 it was held by Miler Magrath, a former Franciscan who had been Rome's Bishop of Down, kept drawing on Roman appointments while holding Cashel, accumulated four dioceses and seventy benefices, and is buried in the cathedral under an epitaph he wrote himself. The rock remained; the ministry on it was for fifty years a scandal. The dictionary records Cashel because a stone fortress named for its own strength is the natural place to say where the church's rock actually is: “and that Rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rock as a large mass of stony matter, figuratively defence or means of safety; a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; and pluralism as the holding of more than one benefice at once.
webster_full: ROCK, n. A large mass of stony matter; in Scripture, defence, means of safety, protection; strength.
BENEFICE, n. [L. beneficium.] An ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue for the maintenance of divine service.
PLURALITY, n. The holding of more than one ecclesiastical living or benefice at the same time by one person.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a fort; a strong hold; a place of defence.
HEWN, participle passive of hew; cut with an edged instrument; shaped by cutting.
scriptures: And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
Isa 51:1
Hearken to me, ye that follow after righteousness, ye that seek the LORD: look unto the rock whence ye are hewn, and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: The Munster archbishopric on the Rock of Cashel, held from 1571 to 1622 by Miler Magrath, who accumulated four dioceses and seventy benefices.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption at Cashel is literal and is the dictionary's own side's to own. Magrath was the crown's archbishop, appointed to carry the Reformation into Munster, and what he carried was pluralism on a scale that would have embarrassed a medieval curia: four sees at once, seventy livings, churches without services, revenues collected and ministry not performed. No account of why the Reformation failed to take hold in Ireland is honest without him in it.

The principle to recover is that the church's rock is a Person and not a place, an institution or a line of succession. Paul identifies the rock of the wilderness outright: “for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4). David piles the words of defence on one object and none of them is a building — “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2). Isaiah tells those who seek the LORD to look back to the quarry they were cut from (Isa 51:1), and the church Christ builds has his own guarantee against the gates of hell (Mat 16:18).

pos: n. (the archbishopric of Connacht in the Irish-speaking west, the most remote of the four Irish provinces)
etymology: From Irish Tuaim, a burial mound or tumulus; the full name Tuaim da Ghualann, the mound of the two shoulders.
biblical_def: Tuam in County Galway was the metropolitan see of Connacht, the poorest and most thoroughly Irish-speaking of the four Irish provinces, where English was barely heard outside the garrisons. Christopher Bodkin held it from 1536 and conformed to every change of religion from Henry VIII to Elizabeth, keeping the see through all of them; the crown valued him because he could preach in Irish and because Connacht could not be governed from Dublin. The deeper problem at Tuam was never the archbishop's conformity but the want of Irish-speaking ministers and of Irish books: there was no printed Irish New Testament until 1602 and no Old Testament until 1685. The dictionary records the see because the promise about God's name runs from the sunrise to the sunset and does not stop at the edge of a language: “From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised” (Psa 113:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines metropolitan as belonging to a metropolis, an archbishop; a province as a country belonging to a kingdom, a district under a governor; and incense as perfume exhaled by fire, an offering.
webster_full: METROPOLITAN, n. The bishop of a mother church; an archbishop who superintends the conduct of suffragan bishops.
PROVINCE, n. [L. provincia.] A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; the district of an archbishop.
INCENSE, n. [L. incensum.] Perfume exhaled by fire; the odours of spices burnt in religious rites; acceptable prayers and praises.
PURE, a. [L. purus.] Separate from all heterogeneous matter; clear; free from moral defilement.
WEST, n. The point where the sun sets at the equinox; the region of the setting sun.
scriptures: From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised.
Mal 1:11

For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the LORD of hosts.

So shall they fear the name of the LORD from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun. When the enemy shall come in like a flood, the Spirit of the LORD shall lift up a standard against him.
Mat 8:11
And I say unto you, That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: The archbishopric of Connacht in the Irish-speaking west, held from 1536 by Christopher Bodkin, who conformed to every change of religion from Henry VIII to Elizabeth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure at Tuam is worth naming exactly, because it is usually described as Irish resistance and was at least as much English neglect. A crown that wanted Connacht reformed appointed archbishops, took the revenues, and did not fund Irish-speaking preachers or print Irish Scriptures for most of a century. The Reformation elsewhere spread by vernacular Bible and catechism within a decade; in Connacht the New Testament arrived in Irish sixty-five years after the break with Rome and the Old Testament a hundred and fifty. That is not a people refusing a book they were offered.

The principle to recover is that God's intention for his name is geographical and total, and the texts say so in the language of sunrise and sunset. The Psalm fixes no limit: “From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised” (Psa 113:3). Malachi promises worship among the Gentiles in every place, with a pure offering (Mal 1:11), and Isaiah has the fear of the LORD coming from the west as well as the east (Isa 59:19). The Lord himself says many will come from east and west to sit down in the kingdom (Mat 8:11).

pos: n. (the Ulster see whose bishop collected the depositions of the 1641 rising)
etymology: From Irish Clochar, a stony place; cloch, a stone.
biblical_def: Clogher is the see straddling Tyrone, Fermanagh and Monaghan. Its bishop from 1645 was Henry Jones, who had been dean there in 1641 when the Ulster rising broke out, and who was taken prisoner by the insurgents and then made chief commissioner for collecting the sworn statements of the survivors. The resulting depositions — thousands of statements taken from Protestant settlers who had been robbed, stripped, driven out or had seen their families killed — are the central and most disputed source for what happened in 1641. They were used at once as propaganda, the numbers inflated by pamphleteers, and the genuine evidence in them dismissed for three centuries as a result. The dictionary records the see because Scripture treats the recording of such things as God's own practice first: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a deposition as the testimony of a witness reduced to writing; inquisition as judicial inquiry, examination; and to avenge as to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party.
webster_full: DEPOSITION, n. [L. depositio.] The act of giving testimony under oath; the testimony of a witness reduced to writing in due form.
INQUISITION, n. [L. inquisitio.] Judicial inquiry; official examination; a court for the examination of heretics.
AVENGE, v.t. To take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injuring party; to vindicate by inflicting pain on the wrongdoer.
BOTTLE, n. A hollow vessel of glass, leather or other material, with a narrow mouth, for holding liquors.
HUMBLE, a. Low; not high; modest; meek; in Scripture, the afflicted, the poor and oppressed.
scriptures: Psa 56:8
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
Psa 9:12
When he maketh inquisition for blood, he remembereth them: he forgetteth not the cry of the humble.
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.
corruption_summary: The Ulster see whose bishop Henry Jones directed the collection of the 1641 depositions, thousands of sworn statements from survivors of the Ulster rising.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The depositions themselves are the contested ground, and the dictionary states its position plainly rather than taking a side's word for it. Two things are true at once. The pamphlet literature built on them grossly exaggerated the numbers killed and used them to justify Cromwell's campaign and the confiscations that followed, and that exaggeration was a real injustice with real consequences. And the depositions are also, as modern scholarship working through the whole archive has confirmed, substantially what they claim to be: sworn testimony of ordinary people about what was done to them.

The principle to recover is that God keeps a record of what is done to the afflicted, and keeps it accurately, which is why the inflation of a true injury is itself an offence. The Psalm makes the record God's own: “Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8). He is said to make inquisition for blood and to forget no cry (Psa 9:12). The martyrs under the altar ask the question openly — “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10) — and the answer is not a counter-massacre but a better-speaking blood (Heb 12:24).

pos: n. (the Cavan see whose bishop learned Irish and had the Old Testament translated into it)
etymology: From Irish An Chill Mhor, the great church; cill, a church or cell, and mor, great.
biblical_def: Kilmore is the see covering Cavan, Leitrim and part of Fermanagh. Its bishop from 1629 to 1642 was William Bedell, an Englishman and former provost of Trinity College Dublin, who did what almost no other bishop of the Irish establishment did: he learned Irish in middle age, required his clergy to use it, preached in it, refused to hold more than one see, lived among his people, and organised and funded the translation of the Old Testament into Irish, completing it in manuscript in 1640. When the rising came in 1641 his Irish Catholic neighbours protected him, and at his funeral the insurgents fired a volley over his grave. The dictionary records the see because Bedell did deliberately what Paul describes: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some” (1Co 9:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a debtor as one who owes something to another, one under obligation; to gain as to win, to obtain by effort; and understanding as the faculty by which the mind apprehends truth.
webster_full: DEBTOR, n. [L. debitor.] One who owes another any thing; one who is under obligation to another.
GAIN, v.t. To obtain by industry or the employment of capital; to win; to obtain or receive, as a convert.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it.
BARBARIAN, n. [Gr. barbaros.] Among the Greeks and Romans, a foreigner; one whose language is not understood.
WEAK, a. Having little physical strength; feeble; in Scripture, not strong in faith or knowledge.
scriptures: To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue.
Rom 1:14
I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians; both to the wise, and to the unwise.
Act 22:2
(And when they heard that he spake in the Hebrew tongue to them, they kept the more silence: and he saith,)
corruption_summary: The Cavan see whose bishop William Bedell learned Irish in middle age, required it of his clergy, and completed an Irish Old Testament in manuscript in 1640.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kilmore is the exception that convicts the rest, and the dictionary uses it that way. Bedell's policy was not clever or novel; it was what every Reformation church in Europe had done as a matter of course. Learn the people's language, preach in it, put the Scriptures into it, hold one charge and live in it. That this was remarkable in the Church of Ireland of 1630, and that his own archbishop and the Dublin administration obstructed the Irish translation, is the whole indictment of the Irish establishment in a sentence.

The principle to recover is that the preacher adapts to the hearer and not the hearer to the preacher, and that this is a debt and not a kindness. Paul is explicit about the method and the aim: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some” (1Co 9:22). He will trade ten thousand words of impressive unintelligibility for five that teach — “Yet in the church I had rather speak five words with my understanding, that by my voice I might teach others also” (1Co 14:19). And he describes himself as owing the debt to the cultured and uncultured alike: “I am debtor both to the Greeks, and to the Barbarians” (Rom 1:14).

pos: n. (the Kilkenny see held for a few months in 1553 by John Bale, who tried to reform it at speed and was driven out)
etymology: From Irish Osraige, the territory of the deer people; os, a deer, with the tribal suffix.
biblical_def: Ossory is the see of Kilkenny, in the old Anglo-Norman heartland of Leinster. John Bale, the English controversialist and playwright, was consecrated its bishop early in 1553 and insisted on the English ordinal against the dean and chapter who wanted the old rite. He preached hard against images and the mass, had his plays performed at the Kilkenny market cross, and alienished almost everyone within months. When Edward VI died in July his servants were killed in the fields, he fled to Dublin and then into exile, and the diocese reverted entirely. Bale's own account of it, the Vocacyon of Johan Bale, is a remarkable and self-justifying document. The dictionary records the see because the lesson is about pace and manner, not about courage: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines forbearing as exercising patience, refraining from retaliation; meekness as softness of temper, mildness, forbearance under injuries; and a season as a fit or suitable time, the convenient time.
webster_full: FORBEARING, participle present. Exercising patience and indulgence; refraining from retaliation or resentment.
MEEKNESS, n. Softness of temper; mildness; gentleness; forbearance under injuries and provocations.
SEASON, n. A fit or suitable time; the convenient or proper time; a period of the year.
STRIVE, v.i. To make efforts; to contend; to quarrel; to struggle in opposition.
PERADVENTURE, adv. By chance; perhaps; it may be.
scriptures: Ecc 3:1
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
corruption_summary: The Kilkenny see held for a few months in 1553 by John Bale, who enforced the English ordinal, preached against the mass, and fled into exile on Mary's accession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is an unfair reading of Bale to refuse before the fair criticism is made. He was not a coward or a hypocrite: he believed the mass was idolatry, said so in a hostile diocese, and his servants paid for it with their lives. The fair criticism stands anyway. He arrived in a diocese whose people he did not know, whose language he could not speak, and in which he had not one ally, and began with a public fight over the ordinal and a frontal assault on the images. Everything he taught about the mass may have been true and none of it was heard.

The principle to recover is that the manner and timing of a reform belong to the reform's substance and not to its packaging. Ecclesiastes is unsentimental about it: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven” (Ecc 3:1). Paul tells Timothy that the Lord's servant is forbidden to be a fighter by temperament — “And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient” (2Ti 2:24) — and that the way to handle opponents is “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25), on the chance God grants them repentance. Proverbs adds the long view (Pro 25:15).

pos: n. (the small County Down see, left nearly empty for most of the Reformation century)
etymology: From Irish Droim Mor, the great ridge; droim, a ridge or back, and mor, great.
biblical_def: Dromore was the smallest of the Ulster sees, a poor diocese in County Down. Through most of the Reformation century it was held in commendam by bishops of other dioceses, left vacant, or given to men who did not reside; the cathedral was a ruin, the parish churches mostly roofless, and the revenues alienated into lay hands before any of the reforming bishops arrived. Jeremy Taylor, bishop from 1661, found a diocese with almost no working ministry and rebuilt the cathedral out of his own means. The dictionary records Dromore not for an event but for an absence, which is the commonest way a church dies: no one does anything to it. Ezekiel puts the charge against shepherds entirely in terms of things not done: “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines commendam as the holding of a benefice in trust until a pastor is provided; to alienate as to transfer title or property to another; and diligent as steady in application, assiduous.
webster_full: COMMENDAM, n. [L.] A benefice or living commended, by the void of a pastor, to the care of a clerk until a regular incumbent is provided.
ALIENATE, v.t. [L. alieno.] To transfer title or property to another; to estrange; to withdraw affection.
DILIGENT, a. [L. diligens.] Steady in application to business; constant in effort; assiduous; attentive.
VACANT, a. [L. vacans.] Empty; not filled; unoccupied with an incumbent or possessor.
IDOL, a. [Gr. eidolon.] An image; in Scripture also used of that which is worthless or good for nothing.
scriptures: Eze 34:4

The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them.
Eze 34:6
My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill: yea, my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek after them.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock! the sword shall be upon his arm, and upon his right eye: his arm shall be clean dried up, and his right eye shall be utterly darkened.
corruption_summary: The smallest Ulster see, held in commendam or left vacant through most of the Reformation century, with a ruined cathedral and alienated revenues.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Dromore is where the dictionary has to say something uncomfortable about its own tradition's record. There is a great deal of writing about Irish resistance to the Reformation and much less about dioceses where the Reformation never actually arrived to be resisted. A see with no resident bishop, no repaired churches, no catechising and no revenue left to pay a minister with had not been rejected by the people of County Down. It had been abandoned by the church that claimed it.

The principle to recover is that the shepherd's sin in Scripture is most often an omission, and that Ezekiel's indictment against the shepherds of Israel is a list of things left undone. Five clauses in a row say what was not done, beginning “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick” (Eze 34:4), and the last of them is the plainest: “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4). The consequence follows as night follows a shut door: “My sheep wandered through all the mountains, and upon every high hill” (Eze 34:6), and the chapter adds that “none did search or seek after them” (Eze 34:6). Proverbs states the positive duty as personal attention — “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — and Zechariah pronounces woe on the shepherd who simply leaves (Zec 11:17).
roots_summary: Hebrew baqash (H1245), to seek or search for; Hebrew 'abad (H6), to be lost or perish.
roots_lines: Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, to search out; “neither have ye sought that which was lost”, Ezekiel 34:4.
Hebrew 'abad (H6) — to perish, to be lost; Ezekiel 34:4.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to search, to inquire after; “none did search or seek after them”, Ezekiel 34:6.
Hebrew yada' (H3045) — to know, to perceive; “to know the state of thy flocks”, Proverbs 27:23.
Hebrew 'eliyl (H457) — worthless, good for nothing, an idol; “the idol shepherd”, Zechariah 11:17.
usage: “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4) — held in commendam or left vacant for most of a century.
“and none did search or seek after them” (Eze 34:6) — the cathedral a ruin and the parish churches roofless.
“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — Jeremy Taylor rebuilt the cathedral from his own means after 1661.

pos: n. (the Donegal see whose bishop ordained Scottish Presbyterian ministers without requiring full conformity)
etymology: From Irish Rath Bhoth, the fort of the huts; rath, a ring-fort, and both, a hut or booth.
biblical_def: Raphoe is the see of east Donegal, and after the Plantation of Ulster its parishes filled with Scottish Presbyterian settlers who had no intention of conforming to the Church of Ireland's ceremonies. Its bishop from 1611 was Andrew Knox, himself a Scot, who ordained Scottish ministers for those parishes on a modified form of subscription, allowing them to state their scruples about the ceremonies and ordaining them anyway, sometimes with Presbyterian ministers laying on hands beside him. George Montgomery in neighbouring Derry and Clogher did much the same. The arrangement held for a generation and gave Ulster a settled Scots ministry; Wentworth and Bramhall broke it in the 1630s by enforcing conformity, and Ulster Presbyterianism became a separate church. The dictionary records the see for what was tried there: “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to subscribe as to sign with one's own hand, to assent to; conformity as compliance with the usages of the established church; and an infirmity as a weakness, a failing, an unsound state.
webster_full: SUBSCRIBE, v.t. [L. subscribo.] To sign with one's own hand; to attest by writing one's name beneath; to assent to.
CONFORMITY, n. Correspondence with a model; compliance with the usages or principles of the established church.
INFIRMITY, n. [L. infirmitas.] An unsound or unhealthy state of the body; weakness; failing; a foible.
SCRUPLE, n. [L. scrupulus.] Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right.
DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words; a controversy carried on in argument.
scriptures: Rom 15:7
Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God.
Rom 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
Rom 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
Php 1:18
What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice, yea, and will rejoice.
corruption_summary: The Donegal see whose bishop Andrew Knox ordained Scottish Presbyterian ministers from 1611 on a modified subscription, an arrangement broken by enforced conformity in the 1630s.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a hard question here that the dictionary will not pretend is easy. Knox's arrangement at Raphoe gave Ulster a working ministry and kept a large Protestant population inside one church; it also asked men to receive episcopal ordination while stating that they did not believe in the office as the church defined it, and both sides knew the formula was doing work the words did not quite bear. Charity that leaves a real disagreement undefined buys time rather than peace, and when Bramhall called the question in the 1630s there was nothing to appeal to.

The principle to recover is nevertheless Paul's, and it is more generous than most parties on either side were: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1). The obligation falls on the stronger party — “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Rom 15:1) — and the pattern of reception is Christ's own reception of us: “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7). Paul can even rejoice where motives are mixed, so long as Christ is preached (Php 1:18).
roots_summary: Greek proslambano (G4355), to receive or take to oneself; Greek asthenema (G771), an infirmity.
roots_lines: Greek proslambano (G4355) — to take to oneself, to receive, to welcome; Romans 14:1 and 15:7.
Greek diakrisis (G1253) — a distinguishing, a dispute, a judging; “doubtful disputations”, Romans 14:1.
Greek asthenema (G771) — a weakness, an infirmity, a scruple; Romans 15:1.
Greek bastazo (G941) — to bear, to carry, to endure; “ought to bear the infirmities”, Romans 15:1.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — a pretext, a pretence; Philippians 1:18.
usage: “Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God” (Rom 15:7) — Scots ministers ordained on a modified subscription from 1611.
“Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Rom 14:1) — Presbyterian ministers sometimes laying on hands beside the bishop.
“We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak” (Rom 15:1) — the arrangement broken by enforced conformity in the 1630s.

pos: n. (the Ulster see and plantation city, walled by the London companies and besieged in 1689)
etymology: From Irish Daire, an oak grove; the London prefix was added in 1613 when the city was granted to the London companies.
biblical_def: Derry was an ancient monastic settlement on the Foyle that became a see, and after the Plantation of Ulster it was granted in 1613 to a consortium of London livery companies, who walled it and renamed it Londonderry. Its bishops included George Montgomery, who like Andrew Knox accommodated the Scottish settlers, and John Bramhall, who did the opposite. In 1689 the city shut its gates against James II's army and held out for a hundred and five days of famine and bombardment, with the rector George Walker as one of its two governors; perhaps a quarter of those inside died. The siege became the founding story of Ulster Protestantism and has been used ever since to sanctify a politics. The dictionary records the city and refuses the use: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bulwark as a bastion, a fortification, that which secures against an enemy; a siege as the setting of an army around a place to compel surrender; and a wall as a work of stone or brick raised for defence.
webster_full: BULWARK, n. In fortification, a bastion, or a rampart; a fortification; that which secures against an enemy.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.
WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, for defence or security.
RULE, n. Government; sway; empire; control; a determinate course of action.
TERRIBLE, a. [L. terribilis.] Dreadful; formidable; adapted to excite terror.
scriptures: Isa 26:1
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
Neh 4:14

And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the Lord, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.
He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
corruption_summary: The Ulster see and plantation city on the Foyle, walled by the London companies from 1613 and besieged for a hundred and five days in 1689.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is a live and current one, and it is not postmodern but tribal. The siege of 1689 has been made into a sacrament: a founding deliverance by which one community in Ulster understands itself as the elect and reads its neighbours as the besiegers in every generation since. The dictionary honours what the people inside those walls endured — a quarter of them died, mostly of hunger and disease — and denies absolutely that their endurance consecrates a political settlement, a parade route or a boundary. A siege is not a covenant.

The principle to recover is that the strong city of Isaiah's song has walls God supplies and not walls men build: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1). The encircling protection in the Psalm is the LORD himself and it is around his people, not around a faction — “so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever” (Psa 125:2). Nehemiah's men do defend their families with weapons in their hands, and he grounds their courage in God rather than in their cause (Neh 4:14). And Proverbs warns what an unwalled city really is: a man with no rule over his own spirit (Pro 25:28).

pos: n. (the Waterford see built on one of the great schools of the early Irish church, long decayed before the Reformation)
etymology: From Irish Lios Mor, the great enclosure; lios, a ring-fort or enclosure, and mor, great.
biblical_def: Lismore on the Blackwater was one of the great monastic schools of the early Irish church, a place men came to from Britain and the continent to study in the seventh and eighth centuries. By the later Middle Ages the school was gone, the see impoverished, and in 1363 it was united to Waterford. At the Reformation the united diocese passed to the Church of Ireland with the usual results: alienated lands, absentee incumbents, and a cathedral in poor repair, while the castle beside it became a Boyle residence. A diocese whose name had once meant a school had no school, and a country that had sent teachers to Europe had to import them. The dictionary records Lismore because the loss of learning in a church is a judgment Scripture names directly: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (Hos 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines knowledge as a clear and certain perception of that which exists or of truth; a famine as scarcity of food, dearth; and a vision as a revelation from God, prophetic sight.
webster_full: KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact; learning; information; skill.
FAMINE, n. [L. fames.] Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
VISION, n. [L. visio.] The act of seeing; a revelation from God; something imparted by supernatural means; prophecy.
MONASTERY, n. [Gr. monasterion.] A house of religious retirement; a convent; a house of religious persons.
PERISH, v.i. To die; to lose life; to be destroyed; to come to nothing.
scriptures: Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
Amo 8:12
And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, they shall run to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, and shall not find it.
corruption_summary: The Waterford see built on one of the great schools of the early Irish church, united to Waterford in 1363 and impoverished by the Reformation century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a romance about early Irish Christianity that Lismore attracts and that should be handled carefully. The schools were real, the learning was real, and Irish monks did carry books and letters back into a Europe that had lost them; the dictionary does not dispute any of that, and does not accept the further claim sometimes built on it, that this was a purer Christianity later ruined by Rome and then by England. What Lismore actually shows is a church that had a great school and lost it, long before either of those parties was in a position to take it away.

The principle to recover is that the destruction of a people for want of knowledge is a judgment, and that the judgment falls first on the teachers. Hosea addresses a priest: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee” (Hos 4:6). Proverbs states it as a law of societies — “Where there is no vision, the people perish” (Pro 29:18). And Amos describes the worst famine as a withdrawal of the word itself: “not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11), after which men run to and fro and do not find it (Amo 8:12).
